s: Every team in this hackathon is bolting an agent onto retrieval.
But an agent is not free.
Every extra step is another model call, more tokens, more latency, and a bigger bill.
So the real question is not whether agentic is better, but whether the extra reasoning is worth its cost.
We tested three standard approaches on the same hundred Olympic questions.
Plain RAG manages sixty three percent, and just ten on counting questions, because the evidence spans up to forty three documents that a top ten retrieval can never hold.
GraphRAG fixes that, but when the graph returns a shortlist instead of an answer, it simply gives up.
The agent fixes that too, reaching a hundred percent, but it pays almost nine hundred tokens on every question, including the ninety seven that never needed it.
This is OCCAM.
Named for Occam's razor: entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity, and neither should retrieval steps.
OCCAM is a controller that sends each question to the cheapest tier that can actually answer it.
Tier zero maps the question to a graph query with no language model. Tier one makes one planning call. Tier two is the full agent loop. Tier three falls back to documents.
A tier only hands over when it can name what it was missing, so evidence is never silently skipped.
Underneath is TigerGraph: over two thousand events, six thousand athletes, venues, sports and countries, as a graph.
Every agent tool is an installed GSQL query on a TigerGraph Savanna workspace, with embeddings stored beside the data as a vector attribute.
We run the same questions through the database and our reference implementation.
Seventy eight questions checked. Zero mismatches.
Now let's run it live. This is the real prototype, replaying recorded benchmark traces.
First, a counting question: how many biathlon events at the twenty eighteen Winter Olympics had more than seventy three competitors?
I press run. RAG retrieves ten chunks and pays almost four thousand tokens, but the answer needs eleven documents, so it fails.
GraphRAG and the agent plan with the language model, spend eight hundred thirty seven tokens, and count inside the database. Correct: five.
OCCAM recognises the shape of the question and answers five, with zero tokens.
Now a harder one. Who won gold in the men's eighty kilogram taekwondo at the Games held just before twenty sixteen?
The graph follows the previous edition edge to London twenty twelve, but finds three candidate events.
GraphRAG stops there. It found the neighbourhood but cannot choose.
The agent resolves it with a second model call, and gets Sebastián Crismanich.
OCCAM reaches the same answer, but skips the replanning: roughly two hundred sixty tokens instead of eleven hundred.
One more: the nordic combined gold before the twenty fourteen Winter Games.
Single pass GraphRAG fails here, and the agent earns its cost by re-planning when the graph reports insufficient evidence.
OCCAM's rules handle this shape directly. Jason Lamy Chappuis, zero tokens.
This is not just a front end. Here is the same taekwondo question, run fresh from the command line against the real code.
RAG is wrong at nearly four thousand tokens. GraphRAG is stuck on the ambiguity. The agent is correct at eleven hundred. And OCCAM is correct at two hundred sixty seven.
Across all hundred questions, here is the tradeoff.

RAG is worst on both axes: sixty three percent at over three thousand tokens. The agent reaches a hundred percent at eight hundred ninety. OCCAM matches it at sixty four tokens, fourteen times cheaper.
By question type, RAG collapses on aggregation and superlatives, while the graph methods hold.
Ninety eight questions never touched a language model. The agent changed the answer on three questions and broke none. Agents are decisive on three percent of questions, and overhead on the rest.
Here is how this maps to what judges care about.
Accuracy: a hundred percent on the public set, with answers for all fifty held-out questions.
Token efficiency: sixty four tokens per question, against eight hundred ninety for the agent.
Completeness: we report evidence recall separately, so an answer without its evidence cannot pass as success.
TigerGraph usage: traversals, GSQL aggregation and vector search in one database, verified against the reference.
And honesty: tier zero is a cache, and on paraphrased questions it falls to tier one, which still answered all six correctly.
Every number is reproducible from the raw run files in the repository.
OCCAM. Know which questions need an agent.
